new_statements.translation: [sec. 3] Kpagua: 32 consonants in 8 places and 7 manners ... 8 vowels. The phonological system of Kpagua is strictly identical to that of Ngundu. ... [sec. 4] Examination of the eleven phonologies presented reveals an obvious relationship. They [have] ... 9 places and 5 to 7 manners. All the languages of this group have open-syllable structure and a three-register tonal system.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kpagua (like the other ten Banda varieties surveyed) is described as a tone language with three level tones and open syllables; the source says nothing about word stress or accent placement. No Kpagua-specific stress statement exists in any source located. (Pan-Banda: Tisserant 1930 pp. 23-24, whose scope explicitly includes the 'Pagwa' of Kouango, adds that Banda has an 'accent d'intensité' on certain syllables with reduction of unaccented syllables, but gives no location rule.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is a group-level generalisation over eleven Banda word lists (Kpagua = 175 citation-form items from Kouango); lexical/citation-form domain; no phrase-level information.
new_statements.identity_note: Cloarec-Heiss 1978's 'kpägùà' = a 175-item list from Kouango (Ouaka, CAR) collected by Bouquiaux & Thomas = Kpagua [kuw], kpag1238; she states its phonological system is 'strictement identique' to Ngundu (ngun1266; Glottolog node Ngundu-Kpagua). Tisserant 1930 treats the 'Pagwa des environs de Kouango' as a small tribe attached to the Yakpwa (Mid-Southern Banda [bjo]); Olson 2001 (citing Fultz & Morgan 1986) reports the DRC Kpagua ('Pagwa' of Van Bulck & Hackett 1956) villages have shifted to Mono [mnh]. The pan-Banda statements on file (Tisserant 1930, Diki-Kidiri & Cloarec-Heiss 1985) are based mainly on Togbo/Linda data; Sampson 1985 is Banda-Tangbago and Cotel 1907 is Togbo — none is Kpagua-specific.

sources.citation: Sampson, Douglas L. 1985. A preliminary phonological overview of Banda-Tangbago. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 4: 133-150. (different Banda variety, Banda-Ndélé group)
sources.note: sec. 5.2: 'Stress is noncontrastive on the word level; it is governed by tone and word shape... In two-syllable words, each syllable is stressed equally... In three-syllable words, the penultimate syllable usually takes less stress than the other two, but will take more stress if it carries the only high tone in the word.' Not Kpagua.

sources.citation: Olson, Kenneth S. 2001. The phonology and morphology of Mono. PhD dissertation, University of Chicago. (Mono = best-described Mid-Southern Banda variety)
sources.note: Kpagua appears only in classification lists and in the Cloarec-Heiss 1978 vowel-system list; quotes Fultz & Morgan 1986 that former Kpagua villages in DRC now speak Mono ('langue morte' on that side of the Ubangi). Mono: three contrastive level tones; no stress/accent statement (only 'stress' hit concerns Selayarese).

sources.citation: Diki-Kidiri, Marcel & France Cloarec-Heiss. 1985. Précis d'orthographe banda. Institut de Linguistique Appliquée, Université de Bangui (colloque, Bangui, avril 1985). 13 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives (image-only PDF; scanned here).
sources.note: Pan-Banda: sec. 1.1 'Toutes les variétés de banda recensées font usage de trois tons ponctuels (haut, moyen, bas) et de deux tons modulés (descendant et montant)'; 1.2 syllables V, CV, CVV, no closed syllables. Nothing on stress/accent (only 'accent aigu' as a diacritic).

sources.citation: Tisserant, Charles. 1930. Essai sur la grammaire banda (Travaux et mémoires de l'Institut d'ethnologie 13). Paris: Institut d'ethnologie. 185 pp. (pan-Banda grammar, main data Togbo/Linda; p. 5 fn. 1 explicitly includes 'la petite tribu des Pagwa des environs de Kouango' with the Yakpwa)
sources.note: pp. 23-24 'ACCENT': every syllable has its own tone (ton haut / moyen / bas); 'En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et ont une tendance à disparaître : Béleda, tronc d'arbre, bleda; temô... tem; marœ, faire, mar.' No rule for where the intensity accent falls.
